summary: This informational memo gives an overview of low-power wide-area network technologies being considered by the IETF. These wireless technologies offer wide coverage, low bandwidth, very small packets and long battery life. It describes their characteristics so protocol work can be informed.

plainLanguage.summary: Low-power wide-area networks let small devices send data over long distances while conserving energy. This RFC compares several technologies and explains why ordinary IP protocols need adaptation for their limits.

questions: what are low power wide area networks
why does ipv6 not fit lpwan
subtitle: An overview of low-power wide-area radio technologies and the challenges of running IP on them.

tldr.problem: Low-power wide-area networks trade bandwidth and packet size for long range and low energy use, while many end devices lack IP support.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Sigfox, and Wi-SUN FAN, then examines gaps between their constraints and existing IETF protocols.
tldr.outcome: This Informational overview is background for work on IPv6 over LPWAN. It describes technologies as understood at publication and defines no protocol.

today: RFC 8376 is an Informational overview published in May 2018. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its descriptions reflect the technologies as presented in the document.

sections.title: What LPWANs Have in Common
sections.content:
LPWAN technologies aim to connect many low-cost devices over large areas while using little power. They accept low bandwidth, small packets, and limits on how often devices may transmit in order to support multi-kilometer radio links and long battery life.

This RFC provides background on technologies considered by the IETF's IPv6 over LPWAN working group and analyzes gaps with existing specifications. Its technology descriptions are informational and are not intended as a comparison of advantages and disadvantages.
sections.plainLanguage: LPWANs save energy and cost by sending small amounts of data over long distances. Their low data rates and transmission limits make ordinary Internet protocols difficult to use unchanged.

sections.title: LoRaWAN and NB-IoT
sections.content:
LoRaWAN uses a star-of-stars arrangement: end devices send radio messages to one or more gateways, which relay them over IP to a network server. Class A devices open two short receive windows after a transmission. The RFC describes very small frame payloads and device-specific session keys.

NB-IoT is a 3GPP technology that uses licensed spectrum and can be deployed in LTE bands or standalone. The RFC reports a 1600-byte MTU, while describing low peak data rates and sleep mechanisms intended to reduce signaling and device power use.
sections.plainLanguage: LoRaWAN devices send to nearby gateways that relay messages to a network server. NB-IoT uses cellular network infrastructure and lets devices sleep between reports.

sections.title: Sigfox and Wi-SUN FAN
sections.content:
Sigfox is based on Ultra Narrow Band radio and is optimized for small, infrequent messages. Under the strictest regulations described, a device may send up to 140 uplink messages and receive up to 4 downlink messages per day.

Wi-SUN FAN is an IPv6 wireless mesh that can use UDP or TCP over IPv6, with 6LoWPAN adaptation and RPL routing. The RFC describes it as the one surveyed technology whose end devices already have IP capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Sigfox is designed for very small, infrequent messages. Wi-SUN uses an IPv6 mesh with routing and transport protocols from the Internet protocol suite.

sections.title: Why Existing IP Protocols Need Adaptation
sections.content:
A basic IPv6 header adds at least 40 bytes, and IPv6 requires a link MTU of at least 1280 bytes. These sizes can exceed LPWAN frame capacities. Neighbor Discovery, DHCPv6, IPsec, and TLS can also require messages and round trips that are costly on constrained links.

6LoWPAN compression can reduce headers, but its fragmentation overhead and Neighbor Discovery exchanges may still be unsuitable for the most constrained links. The RFC also discusses CoAP, routing, mobility, and DNS, noting that a query-response exchange can be problematic when messages are allowed only infrequently.
sections.plainLanguage: IP headers and setup exchanges can be large compared with an LPWAN message. Compression helps, but fragmentation and repeated back-and-forth can still use too much of the network's limited capacity.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The surveyed technologies include authentication or encryption mechanisms defined outside the IETF. The RFC notes that common AAA infrastructure may help manage security across LPWAN deployments.

Encrypted traffic can still reveal activity through when devices send messages. The document says it is unclear whether padding or cover traffic can work in some LPWANs, and notes that certificates and revocation responses are large for bandwidth-limited links.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption does not hide when a device sends a message. Security setup and certificate checks can also be difficult when a network can carry only small amounts of data.
